name: Wiyot
confidence_why: Reichard 1925, the one full grammar consulted, states that no rule for stress placement can be formulated and that accent shifts in connected speech, and Proulx 1984 calls Wiyot stem stress "phonemic underlying", so the lexical reading has no first-hand rival; the only dissent is StressTyp2's tentative weight-sensitive coding of Proulx's historical long-vowel condition, and Teeter 1964, the fullest modern grammar, has not been consulted.

catalog_quote: Reichard 1925:11, §4 ACCENT: "The question of accent in Wiyot is a difficult one. One point is clear, however, namely, that, although stress is of extremely great importance in making the language intelligible, it is not a morphological feature. No rules have been formulated which show where the stress should be placed. Disyllabic words may be stressed on either syllable, and the accent does not remain stable. That is to say, when used independently, a word may be stressed on a certain syllable, but if the same word is found in a sentence the accent may have shifted. The same may be said for polysyllabic words. But should a word have as many as four or five syllables the tendency is toward placing equal stress on the two middle, or approximately middle, syllables. This rule is not by any means absolute. new_statements.quote: [195] 7.1. Stress. A Wiyot stem generally has phonemic underlying stress— manifested, inter alia, when words are cited in isolation—on the reflex of a long vowel if there is one (17,50,66), and otherwise on its first vowel (2,11,21). Stress is acute except in the last syllable of a sentence: there it is acute before a consonant cluster (3,17,47), on the reflex of a short vowel (9), and in absolute word-final position (43,66). It is grave on the reflex of a long vowel before a single word-final consonant (31,45,48). ... [196] When certain suffixes—such as obviative *-V7/i and locative *- Vnki— are added to a Wiyot stem, the position of Wiyot stress generally moves one syllable to the right

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (classification lexical; Reichard 1925:11 quoted, Proulx 1984 p.195 carried from StressTyp2) is confirmed: Proulx calls Wiyot stem stress 'phonemic underlying stress', i.e. lexical, matching WALS 14A 'No fixed stress' / 16A 'Lexical stress' which are sourced to this page. It adds detail the catalog lacks: the diachronic conditioning (reflex of PA long vowel, else first stem vowel), the acute/grave realization in sentence-final syllables, and morphologically conditioned shifts (rightward shift before obviative/locative suffixes, stress-attracting injunctive, always-stressed suffixes). No contradiction with Reichard's 'no rules.. disyllabic words may be stressed on either s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wiyot stems carry phonemic (underlying, lexically specified) stress, heard when words are cited in isolation; diachronically it sits on the reflex of a Proto-Algic long vowel if the stem had one, otherwise on the stem's first vowel, but since Wiyot lost the length contrast the position is not predictable from the Wiyot surface form. Stress is realized as acute pitch except in sentence-final syllables, where acute vs grave depends on the following consonantism and the historical vowel length. Certain suffixes (obviative, locative) shift stress one syllable rightward; the injunctive suffix draws stress toward itself; a few suffixes (items 4, 5, e.g. -Vw 'be') are always stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the recovered text
new_statements.exceptions: stress moves one syllable to the right before obviative *-V?l-i and locative *-Vnki reflexes (cu?l 'maternal aunt' vs the obviative; bas 'fire' vs basakw 'near the fire'); injunctive -it draws stress toward it (item 96); some suffixes are always stressed (items 4, 5); a contracting sequence draws stress from a long vowel for Teeter's informant but not Reichard's (item 114); stress shifts to compensate for loss of *l (item 115)
new_statements.identity_note: Proulx treats Wiyot as a whole (data from Teeter 1964 and Reichard 1925, i.e. the last speakers recorded 1920s-1960s, Humboldt Bay, California) inside a comparative Proto-Algic reconstruction; no dialect distinction is made.

readall_conflicts: The pre-existing disagreement stands as the catalog records it: StressTyp2 codes Wiyot as weight-sensitive (leftmost heavy syllable, else initial, 'tentative') on the basis of Proulx 1984:195, whose 'heavy' is a formerly (Proto-Algic) long vowel, i.e. a historical condition, and who calls the stress 'phonemic underlying'; Reichard 1925 §4 (p.11, read in the original by the catalog) says no placement rules can be formulated and that accent position shifts in connected speech. WALS (14A No fixed stress, 15A Unbounded, 16A Lexical stress, 17A No rhythmic stress, all sourced to Proulx 1984) sides with the lexical reading. Teeter 1964, the best grammar, remains unopened by anyone (lending-only / search-only copies).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Reichard 1925 §4 'Accent' passage is verbatim at p.11 of the held archive.org scanned (line 856 ff.), locator correct; the Proulx 1984:195 leg is honestly marked 'carried' and matches the StressTyp2 passage; (2) Deciding source: a genuine primary reference grammar (Reichard 1925, 215 pp) read in the original, plus a carried comparative sketch (Proulx 1984). It is not the best available description: Teeter 1964 (UCPL 37, 251 pp, Glottolog's top-ranked grammar) has a dedicated treatment of accent phrases/culminative syllable and was not opened on verification, the compilers, or me (all open routes blocked: IA lending-only, Google Books 429, eScholarship WAF, HathiTrust 403). Crossref shows no instrumental or later phonological study of Wiyot prosody (language dormant since 1962), so Teeter 1964 is the ceiling. (3) Risk to the classification: low for the lexical-vs-quantity-sensitive que

sources.note: This work describes Yurok (yuro1248); Wiyot mentioned only as the Algic sister language. Nothing on Wiyot stress, accent or tone. Wiyot appears only as the Algic sister of Yurok (p. 1 and fn. 1), in Goddard's 1975 stem-structure comparison (section 2), in fn. 7 (Wiyot corroboration of the stem-structure scenario is 'conjectural'), and in the summary (section 6). No Wiyot forms are cited. The strings 'stress', 'accent', 'tone' do not occur in the text; the single 'pitch' hit is the gloss 'clear pitch' (resin) in example (19a).
